questions: Why do you think people in cities need public spaces such as parks?
Should local governments spend more money on public spaces or on things like roads and housing?
How have the ways people relax changed compared with your parents' generation?
Some people say that technology makes it harder to relax. Do you agree?
Do you think people in the countryside find it easier to relax than people in cities?
In the future, do you think people will have more free time or less?
tips: Part 3 is about society, not just you: move from personal examples to general trends.
Give a view, a reason and an example, then add a contrast or qualification ('That said...').
It is fine to challenge the question: 'I'm not sure it's either-or...'
Use hedging language for predictions and generalisations: 'I suspect', 'arguably', 'to some extent'.
usefulPhrases: I'd say they're essential rather than a luxury.
I think framing it as a choice is slightly misleading.
That said, I don't think... is to blame.

samples.text:
Q1: Because in the city there are many buildings and not so much nature. People work very hard and they need a place to rest and do exercise. Also for children it is important, they need space for playing because in apartment there is no garden.
Q2: I think both are important. Roads and housing are necessary, of course, because people need to live and go to work. But if the government only build roads, the city will be not nice to live. So maybe they can spend most money for housing and some money for parks.
Q3: I think it changed a lot. My parents when they were young, they relaxed by meeting with neighbours or going to the river. Now young people relax with the phone, they watch videos or play games. They don't go outside so much.
Q4: Yes, I agree. Because with smartphone we always receive message from work or school, even at night. So it is difficult to stop thinking about work. But also technology can help, for example there are apps for meditation.
Q5: Maybe yes. In the countryside it is quiet and the air is clean, so it is easier. But maybe there are not many activities, so some people feel bored.
Q6: I think less, because life is more busy and the work is more competitive. But maybe robots and AI will do some jobs, so maybe more. It is difficult to say.
samples.commentary:
Band 6 overall.
Fluency and Coherence (6): Answers all questions with some development and a willingness to speak at length, although ideas are not always extended far and linking is simple ('Also', 'So', 'But').
Lexical Resource (6): Adequate vocabulary for abstract discussion ('competitive', 'meditation'), with some inappropriate choices ('the city will be not nice to live', 'spend most money for').
Grammatical Range and Accuracy (6): Attempts complex structures (conditionals, comparisons) but makes frequent errors ('the government only build', 'it changed a lot' for a present perfect context, 'more busy', 'receive message').
Pronunciation (6, from transcript only): Assumed generally clear.

samples.text:
Q1: Mainly for wellbeing, I'd say. Cities can be quite stressful, with the noise and the crowds, and parks give people somewhere to switch off. They also bring different groups of people together, so they're good for the sense of community, especially for people who live alone.
Q2: It's a difficult balance. Obviously housing is a priority, particularly where rents are very high. But I don't think it's either-or. A new housing development without any green space can feel quite soulless, so ideally the money for parks should be built into housing projects from the start.
Q3: I think it's become much more individual. When my parents were young, relaxing usually meant socialising, visiting relatives or chatting with neighbours. Nowadays a lot of people relax on their own, with streaming services or social media, which is convenient but arguably less refreshing.
Q4: To some extent, yes. The problem is that we're always reachable, so work and study tend to spill over into our free time. That said, I don't think technology itself is to blame. It's more about how we use it, and some people do switch their phones off deliberately to get a proper break.
Q5: In some ways, yes, because they're surrounded by nature and life tends to be slower. But I'd be careful about romanticising it. Farmers, for instance, often work extremely long hours, so they may actually have less time to relax than an office worker in the city.
Q6: It's hard to predict. Automation could reduce working hours, in theory. But in the past, new technology has often made people busier rather than freeing them up, so I suspect free time won't increase as much as people expect.
samples.commentary:
Band 7 overall.
Fluency and Coherence (7): Speaks at length with coherent, well-extended answers. Uses a range of discourse markers ('That said', 'In some ways', 'in theory') to show stance and contrast.
Lexical Resource (7): Uses less common vocabulary with some precision ('switch off', 'soulless', 'spill over', 'romanticising', 'automation'), and paraphrases effectively.
Grammatical Range and Accuracy (7): Good range of complex structures (passives, 'should be built into', relative clauses) with frequent error-free sentences.
Pronunciation (7, from transcript only): Assumed clear. To reach Band 8, answers would need more speculative depth and more consistently precise vocabulary.

samples.text:
Q1: I'd say they're essential rather than a luxury. Urban life is relentlessly busy, and a lot of people live in small flats without any outdoor space of their own, so a park is effectively their garden. There's also a public health dimension: there's good evidence that access to green space reduces stress, and it encourages people to be more active without them really noticing.
Q2: I think framing it as a choice is slightly misleading. Housing and transport are clearly fundamental, but a city that invests only in those risks becoming somewhere people live out of necessity rather than choice. And well-designed public spaces can actually ease other problems, by encouraging walking, for example, which takes pressure off the roads. So I'd argue they should be treated as infrastructure in their own right.
Q3: The biggest shift, I think, is that relaxation has become far more screen-based and solitary. My parents' generation tended to unwind through face-to-face contact, whether that was a long family meal or an evening at a neighbour's house. Today you can be entertained endlessly without leaving the sofa, which is convenient, but I'm not convinced it's as restorative.
Q4: Broadly, yes, though I'd put the emphasis on how we use it. The constant stream of notifications means our attention is fragmented, and the boundary between work and leisure has become very blurred. Ironically, though, a lot of people now use technology to help them relax, with meditation apps or sleep sounds, so it's a double-edged sword.
Q5: There's a common assumption that rural life is inherently more peaceful, and the surroundings certainly help. But relaxation depends at least as much on time and financial security as on scenery, and people in rural areas often have neither in abundance. So I wouldn't want to generalise.
Q6: Technically, the potential is there, since automation could take over a lot of routine work. Whether that translates into more leisure is really a political and economic question, though. Historically, productivity gains have tended to be absorbed by higher consumption rather than shorter working weeks, so unless attitudes change, I'm sceptical.
samples.commentary:
Band 8 overall.
Fluency and Coherence (8): Develops abstract ideas fully and coherently, challenging assumptions in the questions ('framing it as a choice is slightly misleading') and supporting views with reasons and examples.
Lexical Resource (8): Wide, precise and natural vocabulary ('relentlessly busy', 'public health dimension', 'restorative', 'fragmented', 'double-edged sword', 'absorbed by higher consumption') with skilful paraphrase.
Grammatical Range and Accuracy (8): Wide range of complex structures (conditionals, 'whether that translates into...', 'unless attitudes change') used flexibly, with errors rare.
Pronunciation (8, from transcript only): Assumed easy to understand. Band 9 would need this level sustained with complete naturalness and no loss of precision.
